summary: A percentage is a proportion expressed as parts per hundred: 40% means 40 out of every 100, so it equals 40/100 and 0.40, with 100% as the whole and 50% as half of it. The decisive idea — and the one children most often miss — is that when we find a percentage OF an amount, the percentage acts on a base rather than standing for a fixed amount: 50% is not 'fifty' (it equals 50/100 = 0.5), it is half of whatever the whole is, so 50% of 20 is 10 while 50% of 200 is 100. Teach percentage on the hundred square (40 of 100 shaded) tied to the fraction n/100, the decimal, and a 0%–100% number line, establish landmarks (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) and that percentages can exceed 100%, keep asking '% of what?', and confront base-neglect directly through deliberate comparisons.
misconceptions: Base-neglect: treating a percentage as a fixed number independent of the whole ('50% is always 50 / a lot').
Reading a percentage as a fraction with the number as denominator ('24% means 1/24', '40% means 1/40').
Percentage–decimal placeholder error: writing 9% as 0.9 instead of 0.09.
Believing 100% is the maximum — that you cannot have more than 100%.
Thinking a bigger percentage always means a bigger amount, regardless of the base.

activities.title: Same percentage, different whole: resize the base
steps: Set a percentage (e.g. 50%) and shade that proportion of a 10×10 hundred square.
With the whole set to 20, read off the actual amount (50% of 20 = 10); then change the whole to 200 and read the new amount (50% of 200 = 100).
Describe what stays the same (the proportion / the shaded half of the square) and what changes (the actual amount) as the base changes.
Alongside the shading, write the percentage as a fraction n/100 and as a decimal, and locate it on a 0%–100% number line.
activities.insight: A percentage fixes the PROPORTION of a whole, not a fixed number; the actual amount depends entirely on the base, so you must always ask '% of what?'.

activities.title: Bigger percentage, smaller amount: compare across different bases
steps: Work out 10% of 500 and 80% of 60, showing each amount.
State which is the larger AMOUNT and explain how you know without guessing.
Reflect on why the 'smaller' percentage (10%) gave the bigger amount (50 beats 48).
activities.insight: A bigger percentage does not guarantee a bigger amount, because the amount also depends on the size of the base being taken.

activities.title: Writing and checking the three forms
steps: Shade 40 of 100 squares to match 40%, and simplify 40/100 to 2/5 where asked.

Place landmark percentages on a 0%–100% strip and match them to their fraction and decimal: 100% = the whole = 1, 50% = a half = 0.5, 25% = a quarter = 0.25, 10% = a tenth = 0.1, 1% = a hundredth = 0.01.
Convert single-digit percentages carefully: write 9% as a decimal and as a fraction, and 5% as a decimal.
Decide whether a percentage can exceed 100% and say what 150% would mean.
activities.insight: Percentage, fraction (over 100) and decimal are three names for the same proportion; 'per cent' means parts per hundred, key landmarks (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) link to familiar fractions and decimals, 100% is the whole, and percentages can exceed 100%.

activities.title: Predict, count, reconcile: '50% is always 50?'
steps: PREDICT first: Ann eats 50% of a plate of 10 grapes; Ben eats 50% of a plate of 100 grapes. Since both ate 50%, do they eat the same NUMBER of grapes? Give your reason before working it out.
Then count: Ann eats 5, Ben eats 50.
Reconcile the result with your prediction — same proportion, different amount.
Respond to the claim 'Jo says 50% is always 50': is Jo right, and what does 50% really mean?
Discuss or argue the case 'a 50%-off sale always saves £50' and explain why the saving depends on the original price.
activities.insight: Stating a reason before calculating exposes base-neglect; reconciling prediction with the count cements that 50% is a proportion of a base, not a fixed number.

checkQuestion: Shade 40% of this 10×10 grid, and write 40% as a fraction and as a decimal. Then tell me: Jo says '50% is always 50'. Is Jo right? Explain what 50% really means.
checkAnswer: Shade 40 of the 100 squares; 40% = 40/100 (= 2/5) = 0.40. Jo is wrong: 50% means half of whatever the whole is (fifty parts per hundred), so 50% of 20 is 10 and 50% of 200 is 100 — the amount depends on the base. 100% is the whole; 50% is half of it.
